introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0770 Pure Maths With Statistics 1, June 2019, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL questions: Section A is Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35) and Section B is Statistics (questions 36 to 50). Mathematical tables (formulae booklets) and calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.
incertitudes: Le sujet est un scan sans couche texte (6 pages : page de garde puis 5 pages de questions, filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés), lu page par page en image puis relu en recadrages agrandis (jusqu'à 450 dpi pour les fractions empilées et les symboles). Aucun corrigé ni clé officiels : tous les corrigés sont rédigés et chaque valeur numérique recalculée par script (sympy, scipy et fractions exactes). Aucune constante physique n'est nécessaire. Le sujet compte bien 50 questions : Section A (Pure Mathematics) 1 à 35, Section B (Statistics) 36 à 50 ; aucune page manquante. La page de garde porte « 0770 Math With Statistics 1 », « JUNE 2019 », « ADVANCED LEVEL », « One and a half hours ».
Question 2 : les options A et C sont imprimées toutes deux 2/3 (B = 1/3, D = 3/5) ; seule B est correcte (x = 1/3), la clé reste non ambiguë.

Question 4 : les quatre fractions sont imprimées empilées et serrées ; lues 2/5, 5/2, 5/3 et 3/5 (reconstruites chiffre par chiffre sur un recadrage agrandi). La valeur tan(theta) = 3/5 correspond à l'option D.

Question 7 : les signes moins de l'énoncé sont tombés à la numérisation (« [-2,4] », « f(-2) », « 4-(-2) » lus par cohérence avec le théorème des accroissements finis) ; c = 2 appartient bien à l'intervalle ouvert, option D.
Question 13 : l'option D est lue « (2/x) e^(ln x^2) + k » (écriture peu nette) ; elle n'est de toute façon pas une primitive de x^2, la réponse B reste certaine.
Question 17 : la fraction (1+i)/(1-i) est dégradée sur le scan (lue 1 + i sur 1 - i) ; options lues pi/4, pi/3, pi/2, pi/6. Avec z = i, l'argument est pi/2 (option C).
Question 20 : les exposants des options sont flous sur le scan (lus y^2 = 1 + x^2, 1 - x^2, -1 + x^2, -1 - x^2) ; la solution y^2 = 1 + x^2 est l'option A.

Question 29 : l'option D est imprimée « p (flèche double barrée, pointe à gauche) q » : prise strictement, c'est « q n'implique pas p », ce qui est faux (q => p est vraie), si bien qu'aucune option n'est vraie à la lettre ; la seule affirmation vraie quant au sens (p n'implique pas q) est lue comme l'option D avec une flèche dessinée à l'envers. Question convertie en ouverte (clé non affirmée).
Questions 39 et 48 : le signe « = » (Question 39, E(X) = 18/7) et le « P » (Question 48, P(A union B) = 3/4) sont absents de l'impression ; restitués par cohérence, sans effet sur la réponse.
Question 42 : la moyenne est imprimée « 4 » avec un point parasite devant le chiffre ; lue 4, ce qui donne bien P(0,5 < Z < 1,5), option A.
Question 44 : l'écart type est calculé avec le diviseur Somme f (variance de la population = 708/18 - 36 = 3,33, écart type 1,83) ; l'option A (3,33) est la variance.
Question 49 : la réponse repose sur la table de la loi normale centrée réduite (Phi(0,56) = 0,7123) ; le calcul exact donne a = 0,5601, option C.
Question 50 : le tableau imprimé ne porte pas d'en-tête ; la première ligne (1, 2, 3, 4) est lue comme le rang du juge 1 et la seconde (1, 4, 3, 2) comme le rang du juge 2 (r_s = 0,20, option B).
Question 22 : les constantes s'appellent B et C comme les lettres des options ; sans effet sur la clé (B = -2 et C = -5, option D).

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 29. questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

If $|x+1|<2$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: $|x+1|<2$ means $-2<x+1<2$. Subtracting $1$ from every part gives $-3<x<1$. Check: $x=0$ gives $|1|=1<2$ (true), while $x=1$ gives $|2|=2$, which is not less than $2$, so the end points are excluded. Option A forgets to subtract $1$ (it solves $|x|<2$), and option B is the solution set of the reverse inequality $|x+1|>2$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $x>0$, the value of $x$ for which $\log_4 x+\log_4(6x+10)=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Combine the logarithms: $\log_4\big[x(6x+10)\big]=1$, so $x(6x+10)=4^1=4$. Hence $6x^2+10x-4=0$, i.e. $3x^2+5x-2=0$, which factorises as $(3x-1)(x+2)=0$. So $x=\dfrac13$ or $x=-2$. The condition $x>0$ rejects $x=-2$ (and $\log_4(-2)$ is not defined), so $x=\dfrac13$. Check: $\log_4\dfrac13+\log_4 12=\log_4 4=1$. Options A and C are printed identically ($\dfrac23$), but neither satisfies the equation: $\dfrac23\cdot14=\dfrac{28}{3}\neq4$. **Answer: B.**
Substitute $x=-2$: $f(-2)=(-2)^3-2(-2)-1=-8+4-1=-5$. The common slip is to treat $-2x$ as $-4$ instead of $+4$, which gives $-13$ (option B). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The tangent of the acute angle between the lines $y=4x-3$ and $y=x-5$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The gradients are $m_1=4$ and $m_2=1$. For two lines, $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\dfrac{|4-1|}{1+4\cdot1}=\dfrac35$. Because $\dfrac35>0$ the angle is acute, as required. Option C, $\dfrac53$, is the reciprocal (the cotangent), obtained by inverting the fraction. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The period of the function $f(x)=3\cos 5x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The function $\cos(bx)$ has period $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$; the amplitude factor $3$ does not change the period. With $b=5$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$. Option B inverts the ratio and option C uses the amplitude $3$ instead of $5$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{2x}{(x-3)(x-5)}\equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $\dfrac{2x}{(x-3)(x-5)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{x-3}+\dfrac{B}{x-5}$, so $2x\equiv A(x-5)+B(x-3)$. Put $x=3$: $6=-2A$, hence $A=-3$. Put $x=5$: $10=2B$, hence $B=5$. Therefore the expression is $-\dfrac{3}{x-3}+\dfrac{5}{x-5}$. Check: $\dfrac{-3(x-5)+5(x-3)}{(x-3)(x-5)}=\dfrac{2x}{(x-3)(x-5)}$. Option A drops the sign of $A$ (it takes $\dfrac{2\cdot3}{3-5}$ as $+3$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The function $f(x)=x^3+1$ is continuous in the interval $[-2,4]$ and differentiable on the interval $(-2,4)$. The value of the constant $c$, $-2<c<4$, for which $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(4)-f(-2)}{4-(-2)}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: This is the Mean Value Theorem. $f(4)=65$ and $f(-2)=-8+1=-7$, so the right-hand side is $\dfrac{65-(-7)}{4-(-2)}=\dfrac{72}{6}=12$. Also $f'(x)=3x^2$, so $3c^2=12$, $c^2=4$ and $c=\pm2$. Only $c=2$ lies in $(-2,4)$ (the value $c=-2$ is an end point and is excluded). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An arithmetic progression has first term $\ln 2$ and common difference $\ln 4$. The sum of the first $4$ terms of this progression is
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $S_n=\dfrac n2\big[2a+(n-1)d\big]$ with $a=\ln2$, $d=\ln4=2\ln2$, $n=4$: $S_4=2\big[2\ln2+3(2\ln2)\big]=2(8\ln2)=16\ln2$. Check by listing the terms: $\ln2,\ 3\ln2,\ 5\ln2,\ 7\ln2$, which add up to $16\ln2$. Option A is a different number, $16\ln4=32\ln2$, obtained by mixing $\ln4$ into the formula once too often. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x^2+y^2=16x$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$: $2x+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=16$. Hence $2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=16-2x$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{8-x}{y}$. Options C and D carry a spurious minus sign (the sign that appears for $x^2+y^2=r^2$, where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac xy$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The radius of the circle with equation $x^2+y^2-10x+12y+41=0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Complete the square: $(x-5)^2-25+(y+6)^2-36+41=0$, so $(x-5)^2+(y+6)^2=20$. The centre is $(5,-6)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5$. Equivalently $r=\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}=\sqrt{25+36-41}=\sqrt{20}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A relationship between $(y-2)$ and $(x-1)$ is given by $(y-2)=a\,b^{(x-1)}$. With a suitable linear relationship between $(y-2)$ and $(x-1)$, the intercept of the straight line on the axis of $\log(y-2)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Take logarithms: $\log(y-2)=\log a+(x-1)\log b$. This has the form $Y=c+mX$ with $Y=\log(y-2)$, $X=x-1$, gradient $m=\log b$ and intercept $c=\log a$ (the value of $\log(y-2)$ when $x-1=0$). Option A is the gradient, not the intercept. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{-x}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{-x}dx=\Big[-e^{-x}\Big]_0^1=-e^{-1}-(-e^{0})=1-e^{-1}\approx0.632$. The value must be positive because the integrand is positive, which eliminates B and D; option C exceeds $1$, which is impossible since $e^{-x}\le1$ on $[0,1]$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int e^{\ln x^2}\,dx$
questions.corrige_markdown: Because $e^{\ln u}=u$ for $u>0$, $e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$ (for $x\ne0$). Then $\displaystyle\int x^2dx=\dfrac{x^3}{3}+K$. Options A and C wrongly integrate as if an exponential in $x^3$ were present, and D is not an antiderivative of $x^2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The condition for the quadratic equation $x^2+2kx+(k+6)=0$ to have two unequal real roots is that
questions.corrige_markdown: Two unequal real roots require the discriminant to be strictly positive: $b^2-4ac=(2k)^2-4(k+6)=4k^2-4k-24>0$, i.e. $k^2-k-6>0$, i.e. $(k-3)(k+2)>0$. This holds when $k<-2$ or $k>3$ (outside the roots). Option D includes the equality case, which gives equal roots, and options A and C describe the region where the roots are not two distinct real numbers. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\cos\theta=\dfrac35$ and $\theta$ is an acute angle, then the exact value of $\sin2\theta$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $\theta$ is acute, $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\cos^2\theta}=\sqrt{1-\dfrac9{25}}=\dfrac45$. Then $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2\cdot\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac35=\dfrac{24}{25}$. Option D, $\dfrac{12}{25}$, forgets the factor $2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A $3\times3$ matrix $\mathbf M$ is given as $\mathbf M=\begin{pmatrix}x&1&x-1\\2&1&0\\1&x&0\end{pmatrix}$. If the determinant of $\mathbf M$ is zero, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand along the third column, which has two zeros. The only non-zero entry is $x-1$ in position $(1,3)$, with sign $(+)$: $\det\mathbf M=(x-1)\begin{vmatrix}2&1\\1&x\end{vmatrix}=(x-1)(2x-1)=2x^2-3x+1$. Setting this equal to $0$ gives $2x^2-3x+1=0$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The argument of the complex number $z$, where $z=\dfrac{1+i}{1-i}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $1+i$: $z=\dfrac{(1+i)^2}{(1-i)(1+i)}=\dfrac{2i}{2}=i$. The number $i$ lies on the positive imaginary axis, so $\arg z=\dfrac\pi2$. Alternatively $\arg(1+i)-\arg(1-i)=\dfrac\pi4-\left(-\dfrac\pi4\right)=\dfrac\pi2$. Option A is the argument of $1+i$ alone. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The point $(3,10)$ is on the graph of the function $f(x)$ and $f'(3)=114$. Given that $x=3$ is a first approximate root of the equation $f(x)=0$, using the Newton-Raphson procedure, a value of a second approximation to the root of the equation is
questions.corrige_markdown: Newton-Raphson: $x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. With $x_1=3$, $f(3)=10$ and $f'(3)=114$: $x_2=3-\dfrac{10}{114}=3-0.0877=2.9123\approx2.91$. Option A ($3.09$) comes from adding instead of subtracting the correction, and B ($2.92$) is a rounding error on $2.9123$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A relation $R$ defined on the set of real numbers is such that $x\,R\,y$ and $y\,R\,x\Rightarrow x=y$. $R$ is said to be
questions.corrige_markdown: By definition, a relation is anti-symmetric when ($x\,R\,y$ and $y\,R\,x$) implies $x=y$. This is exactly the stated property. Reflexivity ($x\,R\,x$ for all $x$), transitivity and symmetry ($x\,R\,y\Rightarrow y\,R\,x$) are different properties that the statement does not give. (The relation $\le$ on $\mathbb R$ is an example of an anti-symmetric relation.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $y$ satisfies the differential equation $y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x$. If $y=1$ when $x=0$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Separate the variables: $y\,dy=x\,dx$. Integrate: $\dfrac{y^2}2=\dfrac{x^2}2+c$, i.e. $y^2=x^2+C$. When $x=0$, $y=1$, so $C=1$ and $y^2=1+x^2$. Check: differentiating $y^2=1+x^2$ gives $2y\,y'=2x$, i.e. $y\,y'=x$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that ${}^nC_2={}^nC_3$, the value of the integer $n$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Since ${}^nC_r={}^nC_{n-r}$, the equality ${}^nC_2={}^nC_3$ requires $2+3=n$, so $n=5$. Check: ${}^5C_2=10={}^5C_3$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $x^2-4x-1\equiv(x+B)^2+C$, the values of the constants $B$ and $C$ respectively are
questions.corrige_markdown: Complete the square: $x^2-4x-1=(x-2)^2-4-1=(x-2)^2-5$. Comparing with $(x+B)^2+C$ gives $B=-2$ and $C=-5$. Check by expanding: $(x-2)^2-5=x^2-4x+4-5=x^2-4x-1$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two functions $f$ and $g$ are such that $f(x)=\ln x$ and $g(x)=9-x^2$. The domain of the composite function $fg(x)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $fg(x)=f\big(g(x)\big)=\ln(9-x^2)$. The logarithm is defined only for a strictly positive argument, so $9-x^2>0$, i.e. $x^2<9$, i.e. $-3<x<3$. Option B would result from wrongly requiring $x>0$ as well (that is the domain of $f$ alone, not of the composite), and D is the region where $9-x^2<0$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to3}\left(\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-2x-3}\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Direct substitution gives $\dfrac00$. Factorise: $x^2-2x-3=(x-3)(x+1)$, so for $x\ne3$ the fraction equals $\dfrac1{x+1}$. Hence the limit is $\dfrac1{3+1}=\dfrac14$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{\cos2x}{\cos x-\sin x}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use $\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=(\cos x-\sin x)(\cos x+\sin x)$. Cancelling the common factor $\cos x-\sin x$ (when it is non-zero) leaves $\cos x+\sin x$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coefficient of $x^3$ in the binomial expansion of $(2-3x)^5$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The term in $x^3$ is $\binom53\,2^{5-3}(-3x)^3=10\cdot4\cdot(-27)x^3=-1080x^3$. The sign is negative because $(-3)^3<0$, which eliminates B and D. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^2\dfrac{2x}{1+2x^2}\,dx$
questions.corrige_markdown: The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(1+2x^2)=4x$, so $\dfrac{2x}{1+2x^2}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{4x}{1+2x^2}$. Then $\displaystyle\int_0^2\dfrac{2x}{1+2x^2}dx=\dfrac12\Big[\ln(1+2x^2)\Big]_0^2=\dfrac12(\ln9-\ln1)=\dfrac12\ln9=\ln3$. Option A forgets the factor $\dfrac12$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are given as $\mathbf a=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$. The vector product $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&2&1\\3&1&2\end{vmatrix}=(2\cdot2-1\cdot1)\mathbf i-(1\cdot2-1\cdot3)\mathbf j+(1\cdot1-2\cdot3)\mathbf k=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j-5\mathbf k$. Note the middle term is $-(2-3)=+1$; forgetting the alternating sign for $\mathbf j$ gives option A. Check: $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=3+2-5=0$ and $\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=9+1-10=0$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Statement $p$: $x^2=4$ and statement $q$: $x=2$. The only statement below which is true is

*Options as printed:* A) $p\Rightarrow q$   B) $q\Leftarrow p$   C) $q\Leftrightarrow p$   D) $p\not\Leftarrow q$
questions.corrige_markdown:
If $x=2$ then $x^2=4$, so $q\Rightarrow p$ is true. The converse fails: $x^2=4$ also holds for $x=-2$, so $p\Rightarrow q$ is false. Therefore A ($p\Rightarrow q$) is false, B ($q\Leftarrow p$, which is the same implication as $p\Rightarrow q$) is false, and C ($p\Leftrightarrow q$) is false. The only option that can express a true fact is D, read as \"$p$ does not imply $q$\". In the scan the arrow of option D has its head on the left with a stroke through it; taken strictly, that symbol means \"$q$ does not imply $p$\", which would be false (as $q\Rightarrow p$ holds), so the printed arrow direction is unreliable.

**Intended answer: D ($p\not\Leftarrow q$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: There are $6$ black cards and $4$ red cards on a table. In how many ways can $4$ cards be selected from the table if the number of colours in the selection must be equal?
questions.corrige_markdown: An equal number of each colour among $4$ cards means $2$ black and $2$ red. The number of selections is ${}^6C_2\times{}^4C_2=15\times6=90$. Option A, $15$, is only ${}^6C_2$ (it ignores the choice of the red cards). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equations of the asymptotes of the graph of the curve $y=\dfrac{x-2}{x^2-4x+3}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Factorise the denominator: $x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)$, which vanishes at $x=1$ and $x=3$ while the numerator $x-2$ does not, so these are vertical asymptotes. The degree of the numerator ($1$) is less than that of the denominator ($2$), so $y\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$ and $y=0$ is the horizontal asymptote. Option D wrongly takes $y=1$ (which would need equal degrees). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\sin(x+y)=x$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Differentiate implicitly: $\cos(x+y)\left(1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=1$. Then $1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac1{\cos(x+y)}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\cos(x+y)}-1=\dfrac{1-\cos(x+y)}{\cos(x+y)}$. Option D has the opposite sign. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The relationship between two variables $x$ and $y$ is expressed by the values in the table below.

| $x$ | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 0.693 | 1.099 | 1.386 | 1.609 |

Using the Trapezium rule, an approximate value for $\displaystyle\int_2^5y\,dx$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: There are $4$ ordinates, hence $3$ strips of width $h=1$. Trapezium rule: $\displaystyle\int_2^5y\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\big[y_0+y_3+2(y_1+y_2)\big]=\dfrac12\big[0.693+1.609+2(1.099+1.386)\big]=\dfrac12(2.302+4.970)=\dfrac12(7.272)=3.636$. Option D, $3.663$, is a digit transposition of the correct value. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $z=\dfrac{1+2i}{3-4i}=a+bi$, then $z=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: $z=\dfrac{(1+2i)(3+4i)}{(3-4i)(3+4i)}=\dfrac{3+4i+6i+8i^2}{9+16}=\dfrac{-5+10i}{25}=-\dfrac15+\dfrac25i$. Note $8i^2=-8$, so the real part is $3-8=-5$; forgetting that sign gives option A. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The position vectors of the points $A$ and $B$ are $\overrightarrow{OA}=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=-2\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-2\mathbf k$. A vector equation of the line passing through $A$ and $B$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: A line through $A$ with direction $\overrightarrow{AB}$ has equation $\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OA}+\mu\,\overrightarrow{AB}$. Here $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=(-2-2)\mathbf i+(4-1)\mathbf j+(-2+4)\mathbf k=-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$. So $\mathbf r=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k+\mu(-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$. Check: for $\mu=1$ the line passes through $(2-4,\,1+3,\,-4+2)=(-2,4,-2)=B$. Option A has the direction $4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ (sign error on the $\mathbf i$ component, so it never reaches $B$), and options B and D use the vector $\overrightarrow{OA}$ as the direction and a wrong point, so they do not pass through $A$ and $B$. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: $\mathbf r=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k+\mu(4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=-4\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k+\mu(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k+\mu(-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$
$\mathbf r=-4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j-2\mathbf k+\mu(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k)$

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: STATISTICS**

In a class, $25$ students are offering Economics or Geography or both. If $12$ students offer Economics and $17$ offer Geography, then the number of students offering both subjects is
questions.corrige_markdown: Every student offers at least one subject, so $n(E\cup G)=25$. Inclusion-exclusion: $n(E\cup G)=n(E)+n(G)-n(E\cap G)$, so $25=12+17-n(E\cap G)$ and $n(E\cap G)=29-25=4$. Check: only Economics $=12-4=8$, only Geography $=17-4=13$, and $8+4+13=25$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two independent events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac25$ and $P(B)=\dfrac37$. $P(A\cup B)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: For independent events $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)=\dfrac25\cdot\dfrac37=\dfrac6{35}$. Then $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{14}{35}+\dfrac{15}{35}-\dfrac6{35}=\dfrac{23}{35}$. Option B, $\dfrac{29}{35}$, is the sum $P(A)+P(B)$ without subtracting the intersection. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The mean of a set of $6$ observations is $4$ and the mean of another set of $4$ observations is $6$. The mean of the combined set of observations is
questions.corrige_markdown: The totals are $6\times4=24$ and $4\times6=24$, so the combined total is $48$ over $10$ observations: $\dfrac{48}{10}=4.8$. Option A, $5.0$, is the unweighted average of the two means, which is wrong because the sets have different sizes. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A discrete random variable $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(6,p)$, $0<p<1$. If $E(X)=\dfrac{18}{7}$, then the value of $p$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a binomial distribution $E(X)=np=6p$. Setting $6p=\dfrac{18}7$ gives $p=\dfrac{18}{42}=\dfrac37$, which satisfies $0<p<1$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The mean number of buses arriving at a particular bus stop within an hour is $6$. The probability that no bus arrives at this bus stop within half an hour interval is
questions.corrige_markdown: Arrivals follow a Poisson process. For a half-hour interval the mean is $\lambda=6\times\dfrac12=3$. Then $P(N=0)=e^{-\lambda}\dfrac{\lambda^0}{0!}=e^{-3}\approx0.0498$. Option A uses the full-hour mean $6$, which would apply to an interval of one hour. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The probability density function of a continuous random variable $X$ is defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac3{16}(4-x^2),&0<x<2,\\0,&\text{elsewhere.}\end{cases}$ If the median of $X$ is $m$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: The median $m$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^mf(x)\,dx=\dfrac12$. Compute $\displaystyle\int_0^m\dfrac3{16}(4-x^2)dx=\dfrac3{16}\Big[4x-\dfrac{x^3}3\Big]_0^m=\dfrac3{16}\left(4m-\dfrac{m^3}3\right)=\dfrac{12m-m^3}{16}$. Setting this equal to $\dfrac12$ gives $12m-m^3=8$, i.e. $m^3-12m+8=0$ (the root in $(0,2)$ is $m\approx0.69$). Options B and D (printed identically) have only positive coefficients, so they cannot have a positive root; option C has the wrong constant sign. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A random variable $X$ follows a normal distribution with mean $4$ and standard deviation $2$. $P(5<X<7)\equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown: Standardise with $Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}=\dfrac{X-4}{2}$: for $X=5$, $z=\dfrac12=0.5$ and for $X=7$, $z=\dfrac32=1.5$. So $P(5<X<7)=P(0.5<Z<1.5)\approx0.2417$. Option B would need a lower limit below the mean (that is, $X<4$), option C is its mirror image for $X<4$, and D does not correspond to any standardisation of $5$ and $7$ with $\mu=4$, $\sigma=2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A factory manager claims that the lengths of a certain type of rods produced in his factory have a mean of $420$ cm and a standard deviation of $12$ cm. To test this claim at a $5\%$ level of significance, a sample of $100$ rods was randomly selected and found to have a mean length of $423$ cm. The value of the test statistic for this test will be
questions.corrige_markdown: The population standard deviation is known, so the test statistic is $z=\dfrac{\bar x-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}=\dfrac{423-420}{12/\sqrt{100}}=\dfrac{3}{1.2}=2.50$. (The values $1.96$ and $1.64$ are critical values for a $5\%$ two-tailed and one-tailed test, not the test statistic.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The summary statistics of a data set is such that $\sum f=18$, $\sum fx=108$ and $\sum fx^2=708$. The standard deviation of this distribution is
questions.corrige_markdown: The mean is $\bar x=\dfrac{108}{18}=6$. The variance is $\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{\sum f}-\bar x^2=\dfrac{708}{18}-36=39.33-36=3.33$. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{3.33}=1.826\approx1.83$. Option A, $3.33$, is the variance, not the standard deviation. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A random experiment consists of tossing a coin $10$ times. The random variable \"the number of heads obtained\" can best be described by
questions.corrige_markdown: There is a fixed number of independent trials ($n=10$), each with two outcomes (head or tail) and a constant probability of a head ($\tfrac12$), and $X$ counts the successes. That is a Binomial distribution, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(10,\tfrac12)$. A geometric variable counts trials until the first success, a Poisson variable has no fixed number of trials and an exponential variable is continuous. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A fair die is rolled once. Given that the score is an even number, the probability that it is a prime number is
questions.corrige_markdown: The even scores are $\{2,4,6\}$ and the only prime among them is $2$. So $P(\text{prime}\mid\text{even})=\dfrac{P(\text{prime and even})}{P(\text{even})}=\dfrac{1/6}{3/6}=\dfrac13$. Option D, $\dfrac16$, is the unconditional probability of rolling a $2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The mean of $n$ numbers is $13$. When $27$ is added to the $n$ numbers, the mean of the $n+1$ numbers is $15$. The value of $n$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The sum of the original numbers is $13n$. After adding $27$ the sum is $13n+27=15(n+1)$, so $13n+27=15n+15$, $12=2n$ and $n=6$. Check: $13\cdot6+27=105=15\cdot7$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A')=\dfrac23$, $P(B)=\dfrac12$ and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac34$. $P(A\cap B)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $P(A)=1-\dfrac23=\dfrac13$. From $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$: $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac13+\dfrac12-\dfrac34=\dfrac{4+6-9}{12}=\dfrac1{12}$. Option A, $\dfrac16$, is the product $P(A)P(B)$, which is valid only for independent events (here the events are not independent). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The standard normal variable $Z$ is such that $Z\sim N(0,1)$. If $P(Z>a)=0.2877$, then $a=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $P(Z>a)=0.2877$ gives $\Phi(a)=1-0.2877=0.7123$. From the standard normal table, $\Phi(0.56)=0.7123$ (and $\Phi(0.58)=0.7190$, $\Phi(0.65)=0.7422$, $\Phi(0.71)=0.7611$), so $a=0.56$. The inverse normal value is $0.5601$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
In a certain competition, two judges ranked $4$ contestants as shown in the table below.

| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 3 | 2 |

The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient for this data is
questions.corrige_markdown: The two rows are the ranks given by the two judges. The differences are $d=0,\,-2,\,0,\,2$, so $\sum d^2=0+4+0+4=8$ and $n=4$. Then $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2-1)}=1-\dfrac{6\cdot8}{4\cdot15}=1-\dfrac{48}{60}=0.20$. A negative value (option C) would need $\sum d^2>10$, that is, a ranking that is more reversed than agreeing. **Answer: B.**
